metaTitle: Best Snow Blowers for Hills and Slopes (2026)
metaDescription: Five snow blowers compared for sloped driveways, with self-propelled two-stage gas and battery machines plus two light single-stage options.
expertTake: A sloped drive needs a self-propelled machine, and the EGO SNT2405 is the best battery pick while the WEN SB209E is the best gas pick for the money. The EGO SNT2425 adds a newer kit on the same idea. The two light single-stage machines are only for gentle slopes where you can push the weight yourself. Fit chains before the first icy morning. Practise with the machine on a flat patch first. Buy for the steepest part of your drive.
introParagraphs: Slopes change what a machine has to do. On a flat drive the operator only steers, but on a hill the machine must pull its own weight uphill, hold traction on a slick surface and avoid sliding sideways on the way down. A hill is a safety question as much as a clearing one. Planning for the worst spot makes the rest of the drive easy.

That makes the drive system the main specification, ahead of path width or throw. A self-propelled two-stage with good tires does the climbing for you, while a light single-stage relies on your legs and the grip of your boots. Check the drive and tires first, and the width second. Walk the drive before buying and note the steepest section. A short test pass on a gentle section tells you how the drive feels before you commit to the steep part.

products.name: WEN SB209E 24-inch 209cc two-stage, self-propelled
products.description:
The SB209E is a conventional gas two-stage with a 24-by-20-inch clearing path, a 209cc engine and a self-propelled drive with six forward and two reverse speeds. WEN rates it for over 2,000 pounds of snow per minute and a throw of up to 30 feet.

Self-propelled drive is the reason it suits hills. The wheels pull the machine uphill and the speed range lets you slow down on a descent, which keeps the operator from being dragged. The 190-degree chute lets you throw downhill without stopping.

Electric start is useful on a cold slope. Keep fresh fuel, check the oil and consider chains for the tires on glare ice. Check the garage door and any ramp before ordering, because the machine is heavy and a slope makes it harder to move. Many owners fit tire chains for glare ice before the first storm. It also helps that the chute rotates far enough to throw downhill without turning the whole machine.
products.bestFor: Sloped gas drives where self-propelled drive is the main need.
pros: Self-propelled with six forward and two reverse speeds

products.name: EGO SNT2405 24-inch self-propelled two-stage kit, 2 x 7.5Ah
products.description:
The SNT2405 is a battery two-stage with variable-speed self-propelled drive, a 24-inch path and a 20-inch intake. The listing rates it for an 18-car driveway in 8 inches of snow on two packs.

For a hill, the variable speed is the valuable feature. You can crawl uphill when the load is heavy and speed up on the flat, and the machine holds a line without the operator pulling. Packs drain faster on a climb, so expect fewer cars per charge than the listing.

Store the packs indoors and charge them before the forecast. It is a quiet choice for early starts on a slope. Because the climbs drain packs faster, keep a spare pair charged and use the lower speed on the hill to save runtime. A cold pack can look weaker, so bring both inside between sessions. The variable drive lets you ease off on a steep stretch, which is the single most useful control on a hill.
products.bestFor: Sloped drives where quiet, fuel-free operation matters.

products.name: EGO Power+ SNT2425 24-inch two-stage kit, 2 x 7.5Ah
products.description:
The SNT2425 is the newer 24-inch EGO two-stage, with two 7.5Ah packs and Peak Power mode. The listing claims an 18-car driveway in 8 inches of snow and a 50-foot throw.

It shares its class with the SNT2405, so the choice is largely about which version is available and what the box contains. For a hill, the same logic applies: choose the self-propelled drive and expect shorter runtime on climbs.

Consider a spare pair of packs if your slope is long. If you are choosing between the two EGO kits, compare what is in each box and whether the packs and charger are included, since the machine is otherwise the same class. Its Peak Power mode helps when a wet berm crosses the slope, though it drains the packs quickly.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the current EGO 24-inch kit for a slope.
pros: Peak Power mode for heavy loads

products.name: Greenworks 40V 16-inch brushless snow blower, tool only
products.description:
This is a light single-stage with no wheel drive, so it relies on you to push it uphill. It makes sense only on a gentle slope where a small machine and good boots can manage.

Its advantage is weight: it is easy to carry and turn on a slippery grade. A 16-inch path and a 10-inch depth suit light snow, and the listing is tool only, so battery and charger are extra.

For a steep hill, choose a self-propelled two-stage instead. If you already own 40V packs, the bare tool is the cheapest way to get a very light machine for a gentle grade. It is the pick when you need to carry the machine up steps to a hillside property.
products.bestFor: Gentle slopes where a light machine is easier than a heavy one.

products.name: Snow Joe IONMAX 24V-X2-SB18-GO 18-inch cordless blower
products.description:
The SB18-GO is an 18-inch cordless single-stage with a 1,200 watt brushless motor and a stated 700 pounds per minute. It has a 180-degree chute and throws about 20 feet.

Like the Greenworks, it has no wheel drive, so it suits a gentle grade only. The light frame makes it easier to control on a slope than a heavy two-stage you would have to hold back.

For a steep or long hill, move up to a self-propelled model. Ask the seller about warranty and replacement paddles, and keep the plastic auger away from gravel patches on the slope. It is the cheapest way to try a battery machine on a modest grade.
products.bestFor: Gentle slopes and short hills with light snow.
cons: Plastic auger wears on rough surfaces

buyingCriteria.explanation: On a hill, a machine that pulls itself is worth more than extra width or throw. The WEN, EGO SNT2405 and SNT2425 all have powered wheels. A hand-pushed single-stage forces you to push or restrain the machine, which is tiring and unsafe on ice. Many buyers focus on width and throw and forget the drive, and only learn on the first icy morning that a hand-pushed machine slides back down. Test the drive on a gentle slope before you rely on it. Add a bag of grit or salt to the kit, because no machine replaces traction on a bare ice patch.

The WEN offers six forward and two reverse speeds, and the EGO uses variable speed. A wide range lets you crawl uphill under load and slow down on a descent. Reverse gears help you back out of a drift on a slope. A wider speed range also helps on the flat, where you can speed up on light snow and slow down on heavy snow. Reverse gears help you back out of a drift without lifting the front of the machine. Note that a self-propelled drive is usually adjustable, so practise on the flat to learn how it feels before you try it on the hill.

Knobby snow tires bite into packed snow, but glare ice defeats most tires. Chains or tracks add grip on slick slopes. Check whether tire chains are an option for your machine before the first storm. If your slope has an icy patch that never melts, chains or a sprinkle of grit under the tires will do more than any engine upgrade. Check the clearance before fitting chains. A tire that grips on packed snow can skate on thin ice, so pick chains or studs if your slope ices over.

A heavy two-stage pulls itself but is harder to restrain going downhill, while a light single-stage is easy to move but needs your muscle. A self-propelled machine with a low center of gravity is the safest. A heavy machine has more traction but more momentum, which is why the descent is the dangerous part. Keep a firm grip, work slowly and never walk in front of the machine going downhill. A light single-stage can be easier to control on a short slope, but only if you are strong enough to hold it back.

Climbing draws more power. A gas engine copes with load easily, while battery packs run for less time than the listing rates. Plan on a spare pair of packs for a long slope. On a long slope, plan your charging routine around the climb, because the battery will run down faster than on a flat drive. Gas gives you more margin. Rotate packs between climbs so that neither runs down first.

On a slope you want to throw snow downhill and away from the drive. A chute that rotates through a wide range, like the WEN's 190 degrees, lets you aim without stopping. Throwing downhill is easier and uses less power, so work from the top down where you can. Aim the chute away from the road and neighbours. Aim the chute downhill and clear from the top, so the machine is never throwing snow up the slope. A clear throw path also keeps the machine from burying itself.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drive system
howWeEvaluated.description: We split the lineup into self-propelled two-stage and hand-pushed single-stage machines. On a hill, drive is the deciding feature. On a slope, the wrong drive makes every other spec irrelevant. A slope amplifies every weakness in a machine, so a feature that is minor on the flat becomes decisive on a hill.

howWeEvaluated.title: Traction and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared drive speed ranges of six forward and two reverse against variable speed. A wide range controls the machine on a descent. Speed control matters as much as pull on the descent. We read the six forward and two reverse speeds as a control feature as much as a power feature.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power under load
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how gas and battery cope with a climb. Gas holds power longer; battery runtime shortens. A climb shows how much reserve a power source has. Gas engines keep their output; battery output sags as the pack drains.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership burden
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed fuel upkeep, pack care and wear. A drive belt and tires are the wear items that matter most on hills. On a slope, a broken belt or worn tire is a safety problem as well as an inconvenience.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to slope
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each model to a gentle or steep slope. This is an editorial assessment, not a measured score. We recommend picking for the steepest section of the drive. We assumed a slope of moderate steepness for ranking.

cards.label: Self-propelled
cards.text: The WEN and both EGO models pull themselves uphill and give you speed control on the way down.

cards.label: Hand-pushed
cards.text: The Greenworks and Snow Joe are light and cheap but rely on your effort and grip. Do not use a hand-pushed machine on a steep grade.

howToChoose.note: Pick self-propelled for anything steeper than a gentle slope.

howToChoose.intro: Gas and battery handle load differently on a climb.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Tire chains or tracks, a speed range for controlled descent and a machine with weight. Glare ice defeats plain tires.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The WEN SB209E has the speed range and a gas engine for sustained climbs, and the EGO SNT2405 offers variable speed. Chains cost little and help a lot.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your slope is steep or long. A self-propelled two-stage is the safe choice.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your slope is gentle. A light single-stage will do. Safety is worth more than a saving.

maintenance.why: Traction is the key spec on a hill. Fit chains before the first ice. Test the grip before the first storm.
A worn belt slips on a climb. Replace a belt that shows cracks or glazing. Look for glazing on the belt.
Fresh oil protects the engine under load. Fresh oil helps a hard-working engine. Check the level after a few hours of climbing. Check the engine mount bolts while you are there.
Cold reduces output. A warm pack climbs better. Store packs warm and dry.
Pins protect the gearbox. Carry spares in the garage. Keep the shoes adjusted for the surface. Wait for the auger to stop before touching anything.

faq.q: Do I need a self-propelled machine on a hill?
faq.a: On anything steeper than a gentle slope, yes. A hand-pushed machine is tiring and can slide. If you are unsure, choose self-propelled; the cost of the wrong choice is a fall. Many owners also add a handrail on steep steps beside the drive.

faq.q: Gas or battery on a slope?
faq.a: Gas holds power under load. Battery is quieter but climbs drain packs faster. Many owners keep a bag of salt or grit by the door as well. Gas is the easier choice for a long slope.
On glare ice, yes. Chains add grip where plain tires fail. Chains are cheap and quick to fit once you have tried it. Salt or grit helps too.

faq.q: Which way should I work on a slope?
faq.a: Work across or downhill where possible and throw snow downhill and away from the path. Starting at the top is safer because the machine pulls away from you. A zigzag pattern on a steep slope reduces the load.

faq.q: Can a single-stage handle a hill?
faq.a: Only a gentle one. It relies on your effort and boot grip. A light machine suits a gentle grade where you can keep your footing. Hand-pushed machines are for gentle slopes only.

If you cannot walk it safely, a machine will not make it safer. Add salt and traction aids. Safety on the slope comes before clearing speed. Ask a neighbour or a dealer if you are unsure how steep is too steep. A cleared slope still needs salt or grit afterward.
